summary: This note is a Wikipedia-derived article on Apollo, covering the uncertain etymology of his name (Greek, Doric Apellon, and possible Hittite, Hurrian, Etruscan and Akkadian links) and his role as a god of plague and healing. It also describes his functions as oracular patron of Delphi, protector of herds and colonists, and leader of the Muses, as well as Plato's theory of forms as a contrasting philosophical note. The text is a dense overview of how these roles were fused in his cult.
one_line: Overview of Apollo's uncertain name etymology and his roles as god of plague, healing, prophecy at Delphi, and music and poetry.
key_facts: The spelling Ἀπόλλων had almost superseded all other forms by the beginning of the common era.
The Doric form Apellon (Ἀπέλλων) is more archaic, derived from an earlier *Ἀπέλjων.
Apella (Ἀπέλλα) was the name of the popular assembly in Sparta, corresponding to the ecclesia.
R. S. P. Beekes rejected the connection of the theonym with the noun apellai and suggested a Pre-Greek proto-form *Apalyun.
The Hittite form Apaliunas is attested in the Manapa-Tarhunta letter.
Aplu was a god of plague in Hittite and Hurrian belief, invoked during plague years in the Late Bronze Age (1700 to 1200 BCE).
Aplu Enlil, meaning 'the son of Enlil', was a title given to the god Nergal, who was linked to the Babylonian sun god Shamash.
Chryses, the Trojan priest of Apollo, invoked Apollo Smintheus ('mouse Apollo') to send a plague against the Greeks.
Homer interprets Apollo as a terrible god (δεινὸς θεός) who brings death and disease with his arrows but can also heal.
Apollo Smintheus retained an older agricultural function as protector from field rats.
The healer-god Paean seems to have Mycenean origin, and his functions were fused in the cult of Apollo.
As the patron of Delphi (Pythian Apollo), Apollo was the prophetic deity of the Delphic Oracle.
Medicine and healing are associated with Apollo, either through the god himself or through his son Asclepius.
Apollo led the Muses as Apollon Musegetes and directed their choir, making him patron god of music and poetry.
Hermes created the lyre for Apollo, and the instrument became a common attribute of Apollo.
Hymns sung to Apollo were called paeans.
Plato extended the Greek belief of ideal forms into his metaphysical theory of forms (ideai, 'ideas').
